title: The kingfisher and the bullet train
where_you_might_see_it: A sudden flash of electric blue darting low over a river or canal — kingfishers live all across the UK wherever the water is slow and clean. Look for them on riverbanks and canal towpaths, especially in autumn and winter.
natures_problem: To catch a fish, a kingfisher has to dive straight from the air into the water. But hitting water usually makes a big splash — and a splash warns the fish, which darts away.
natures_solution: The kingfisher's long, pointed beak is shaped so that it slips from the air into the water almost without a splash. The fish never sees it coming.
what_people_made: In Japan, an engineer who loved birdwatching was trying to fix a high-speed 'bullet train' that made a loud BANG every time it shot out of a tunnel. He gave the train a long, pointed nose shaped just like a kingfisher's beak — and the bang disappeared. The train became faster and quieter too.
try_this: Fill a sink with water. Drop in a round pebble, then drop a pencil in point-first. Which one makes the bigger splash? Why might a long, pointed shape be better for diving?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Forces — air resistance, water resistance, and streamlining
curriculum_links.how: The kingfisher's tapered beak is a vivid, real-world example of how a streamlined shape reduces resistance when moving from air into water — ideal for introducing forces and drag in Year 5.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — evaluate and improve existing products using learning from nature
curriculum_links.how: Engineers studied the kingfisher's beak and redesigned the bullet-train nose, demonstrating the DT cycle of evaluating a problem, learning from nature, and iterating a design to improve performance.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Animals including humans — animal adaptations and habitats
curriculum_links.how: The kingfisher's beak is an adaptation that allows it to dive from air into water with minimal splash — a clear example of how body structures are shaped by the environment and feeding behaviour.

curriculum_links.subject: English
curriculum_links.topic: Writing — non-chronological reports and explanatory texts
curriculum_links.how: The kingfisher-to-bullet-train story is a compelling narrative for writing an explanatory or persuasive text about biomimicry, giving pupils a real cause-and-effect example to explain and argue from.

image_idea: A kingfisher mid-dive, beak-first, shown side by side with the pointed nose of a bullet train — the same shape twice.

title: The lotus leaf that never gets dirty
where_you_might_see_it: Lotus flowers grow in ponds and water gardens — you might spot them in a botanical garden or garden centre. They rise out of muddy water yet their leaves always look perfectly clean. You can also see a similar trick on the leaves of your garden nasturtiums or a cabbage — watch how water rolls off in perfect silver balls.
natures_problem: The lotus plant lives in muddy ponds. Its leaves ought to be permanently covered in dirt, which would block sunlight and stop the plant making food. Getting dirty could slowly kill it.
natures_solution: Look very closely at a lotus leaf and you'll see it's covered in tiny, tiny bumps — too small to see without a microscope. These bumps are coated in wax. When a water droplet lands, it can only rest on the very tips of the bumps, so it rolls off instantly, taking any dust and mud with it. The leaf cleans itself every time it rains, without the plant doing a thing.
what_people_made: A German scientist noticed this trick and worked out how to make paint that does the same thing. Lotusan paint — used on the outside of buildings — has a rough, waxy surface. Rain rolls off the walls and carries the dirt away, so the building stays clean for years without being washed. The same idea is used in self-cleaning windows and on solar panels — where keeping clean means making more electricity.
try_this: Find a fresh cabbage leaf or a nasturtium leaf in the garden. Drip some water onto it. What shape does the water make? Now try the same on a plain piece of paper. What's different, and why?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — comparing properties of materials including their interaction with water
curriculum_links.how: The lotus leaf's waxy micro-bumps make water bead and roll off, providing a concrete, observable introduction to water-repelling materials and why surface texture affects how water behaves.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: States of matter — properties of liquids and how liquids behave on surfaces
curriculum_links.how: Observing water drops beading on a lotus-effect surface illustrates how surface properties affect liquid behaviour — a hands-on hook for exploring the properties of liquids in Year 4.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — selecting appropriate materials for a function
curriculum_links.how: Lotusan self-cleaning paint shows pupils how understanding a material's surface structure at a microscopic level informs better product design — a real example of material selection solving a practical problem.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptation and survival
curriculum_links.how: The lotus leaf's self-cleaning surface is an adaptation that keeps the leaf free of fungi and dirt in muddy water, helping pupils see how plant structures can be shaped by natural selection for survival.

image_idea: A close-up of a lotus leaf with a perfect silver bead of water sitting on its surface, alongside a diagram showing the tiny waxy bumps underneath — magnified so children can see the structure.

title: The gecko that walks up walls
where_you_might_see_it: Tokay geckos live in tropical forests and warm buildings across South-East Asia — not in the UK. But if you've ever seen a spider walk up a wall, or watched a fly land on a window, you've seen a smaller version of the same mystery: how does an animal stick to a smooth surface without glue? Imagine a lizard the size of your hand doing the same thing.
natures_problem: A gecko needs to chase insects across smooth walls and ceilings. If it slips, it falls. And it can't use sticky glue — it needs to pick up its feet and move them again in an instant.
natures_solution: Each of the gecko's toes is covered in millions of hair-like bristles, so tiny you'd need a microscope to see them. At the very tip of each bristle are even tinier paddle shapes. There are so many of them that together they create a very gentle invisible pull — like the force that makes two pieces of glass stick together when they're wet. The gecko just peels its toes away to let go, instantly and cleanly, leaving no sticky mess behind.
what_people_made: Scientists have been trying to copy this trick to make a tape that you can stick, peel off, and reuse thousands of times without any glue — and without leaving any marks. Space agencies are interested in it for robot arms that can grip satellites without damaging them. Surgeons want a version that could close wounds without stitches or staples. It's still being developed, but some gecko-inspired films are already available.
try_this: Press two small pieces of clean glass together gently. Do they seem to stick a little? Now slide them apart. The tiny invisible pull you felt is the same kind of force the gecko uses — just a million times stronger because the gecko has millions of tiny surfaces all working together.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Animals including humans — how animal body structures are suited to their environment
curriculum_links.how: Gecko toe pads are a striking example of an animal structure perfectly matched to its environment — clinging to vertical surfaces without glue — giving pupils a memorable hook for studying adaptation.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — comparing materials by their properties
curriculum_links.how: The gecko's adhesion works through surface structure rather than sticky chemistry, introducing the idea that how a material is shaped at a tiny scale can change what it can do — a gateway to thinking about material properties beyond simple categories.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — applying understanding of computing, science, and mathematics to solve problems
curriculum_links.how: Gecko-inspired adhesives used in robotic grippers and medical dressings show pupils how understanding nature at a microscopic level leads to genuinely new products, linking DT to science investigation.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptation to environment
curriculum_links.how: The gecko's microscopic toe hairs are an evolutionary adaptation allowing survival in habitats inaccessible to competitors — an excellent example of how structures at a scale we cannot see with the naked eye underpin an animal's survival strategy.

image_idea: A tokay gecko climbing a vertical glass surface, with an inset circle showing a hugely magnified view of the toe bristles — thousands of tiny hairs branching into even tinier paddles.

title: The whale that improved the wind turbine
where_you_might_see_it: Humpback whales live in all the world's oceans and migrate past the coasts of Britain — whale-watching trips from Cornwall, Wales, and Scotland sometimes spot them. They're the size of a bus and famous for their spectacular leaping and singing. Despite being enormous, they can spin and twist in tight circles to herd fish — and their fins are why.
natures_problem: A humpback whale is huge and heavy, yet it needs to make sharp, quick turns to herd fish into a ball before rushing through them with its mouth open. How can something that massive turn so neatly?
natures_solution: The humpback's front fins have a row of bumps along the leading edge, a bit like knuckles. These bumps break up the water flowing over the fin in a way that stops it from suddenly 'stalling' and losing grip. Instead of sliding sideways when it tries to turn sharply, the fin holds on — letting the whale carve tight circles that would be impossible with a smooth fin.
what_people_made: Engineers in Canada noticed these bumps and tried adding the same knobbly pattern to wind turbine blades. In wind-tunnel tests, the bumpy blades produced more power and made less noise than smooth blades. Some large ceiling fans now use the same idea and use about one fifth less electricity than ordinary fans. Quieter, more efficient wind turbines could help us generate more clean energy.
try_this: Hold a flat piece of card in a breeze and angle it so the air flows over it. At what point does it suddenly lose lift and flap? Now try gently crimping one edge into small waves. Does the card hold its angle better? You're recreating the whale's fin experiment.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Forces — air resistance and how shape affects movement through fluids
curriculum_links.how: The tubercles on a humpback whale's fin reduce drag and improve lift, directly paralleling the Year 5 topic of how shape affects movement through water and air, with a memorable mega-fauna example.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Living things and their habitats — adaptation and feeding behaviour
curriculum_links.how: The tubercles allow humpbacks to make tight turns when corralling fish during bubble-net feeding — a vivid link between body structure, hunting strategy, and survival that brings adaptation to life.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — evaluate existing products and learn from natural systems
curriculum_links.how: Wind turbine blades shaped after humpback fins generate more electricity with less noise — pupils can see how a design improvement borrowed from a whale solves a real engineering problem.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Human and physical geography — renewable energy and sustainable development
curriculum_links.how: The tubercle-inspired wind turbine is a clear real-world link between geographical understanding of the need for renewable energy and the role that nature-inspired design plays in making that energy more efficient.

image_idea: A humpback whale's front fin showing the row of bumps along the leading edge, placed side by side with a wind turbine blade with the same knobbly profile along its front edge.

title: The termite mound that inspired a building with no air conditioning
where_you_might_see_it: Termites are not found in the UK, but you'll find their extraordinary towers all across Africa — some more than three metres tall and built by insects smaller than your little finger. Think of how remarkable that is: millions of tiny creatures, none of them in charge, building something as tall as a room and cleverer than most modern buildings.
natures_problem: Termites need to keep their underground nest at almost exactly 31 degrees Celsius at all times — not too hot, not too cold — to keep their fungus gardens and their queen healthy. But in Zimbabwe, where these termites live, the outside temperature swings from near freezing at night to scorching hot in the afternoon.
natures_solution: The mound is riddled with a network of tunnels and chimneys. As the termites' bodies warm the air inside, that warm air rises and escapes through vents at the top, drawing in cooler fresh air from below. The thick earthen walls soak up heat during the day and release it slowly at night, acting like a giant storage heater in reverse. The result is a near-constant temperature inside — no fans, no electricity, no air conditioning needed.
what_people_made: In 1996, an architect named Mick Pearce used these same ideas to design a large shopping centre and office block in Harare, Zimbabwe — the Eastgate Centre. Thick concrete walls and floors soak up the day's heat; ducts at floor level and chimneys in the roof drive fresh air through the building all day and night. The Eastgate Centre uses up to a third less energy than comparable buildings nearby, saving millions of pounds in electricity over the years.
try_this: On a sunny day, press your hand against a brick wall in the morning and again in the late afternoon. What do you notice? The bricks have been storing the sun's heat all day — just like the termite mound. Come back in the evening to feel the wall releasing it.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: States of matter — how temperature changes affect materials and the role of heat transfer
curriculum_links.how: The termite mound maintains a near-constant internal temperature despite extreme daily swings outside — a compelling, animal-built example of insulation and heat transfer that anchors Year 4 States of Matter study.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Living things and their habitats — how animals modify their environment to survive
curriculum_links.how: African termites engineer their own climate-controlled habitat, demonstrating that animals do not simply adapt to their environment but can reshape it — a high-level concept ideal for Year 6 enrichment.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Human and physical geography — climate zones, Africa, and sustainable development
curriculum_links.how: The Eastgate Centre in Harare uses termite-mound principles to cool a building without air conditioning in a hot climate, linking geographical knowledge of Africa and climate zones directly to sustainable architecture.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — sustainable design solutions inspired by natural structures
curriculum_links.how: The Eastgate Centre's passive cooling system — no air conditioning, lower energy use — gives pupils a clear, real-world example of how copying a natural structure produces a sustainable and innovative building design.

image_idea: A tall African termite mound with arrows showing warm air rising and cool air flowing in at the base, placed beside the Eastgate Centre building in Harare with the same arrows showing how air moves through its walls and roof.

title: The shark skin that stops germs spreading
creature: Shortfin mako shark (Isurus oxyrinchus) and related species
where_you_might_see_it: Sharks are not found in UK rivers, but several species — including blue sharks and basking sharks — swim in British coastal waters. You're most likely to see a basking shark off the coasts of Cornwall, Scotland, or the Isle of Man in summer. If you've ever stroked a dried piece of sharkskin, you'll have felt that it's rough like sandpaper in one direction, because of thousands of tiny tooth-like scales all pointing the same way.
natures_problem: A shark needs to slip through the water as quickly and efficiently as possible to catch prey — but it also lives in an ocean full of bacteria that could cause infections. How does it stay both fast and healthy?
natures_solution: Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny ridged scales, each shaped a bit like a small tooth. These ridges run along the direction the shark swims, which helps reduce the drag of the water. But here's the clever extra trick: the ridges also make it very hard for bacteria to find a flat place to grip onto and settle. The germs simply can't get a foothold — no chemicals needed, just the shape of the surface.
what_people_made: Scientists copied the shark's ridged pattern to make a film called Sharklet. It has millions of tiny diamond-shaped ridges — much too small to see with the naked eye. In laboratory tests, up to 99% fewer dangerous bacteria, including the hospital superbug MRSA, were able to grow on Sharklet surfaces compared with plain surfaces. Hospitals are already using Sharklet film on surfaces and medical equipment. Because no chemicals are involved, bacteria can't develop resistance to it — unlike antibiotics. Elite swimmers have even used sharkskin-inspired swimsuits to move faster through the water.
try_this: Look at two surfaces: a smooth piece of card and a piece of corrugated cardboard. Now imagine you're a tiny bacterium trying to settle down and build a home. Which surface would be easier to grip onto? Why might lots of ridges and bumps make it harder for bacteria to stick?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — how surface structure can change material behaviour
curriculum_links.how: Sharklet shows that tiny ridges on a surface — not chemicals — can stop bacteria sticking, helping pupils understand that material properties depend on structure and not just chemical composition.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Animals including humans — microorganisms and health
curriculum_links.how: Sharklet's ability to prevent harmful bacteria such as MRSA from colonising surfaces without using antibiotics is a real-world hook for discussing microorganisms, disease, and why antibiotic resistance matters.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Forces — drag reduction in water, streamlining
curriculum_links.how: Shark-skin riblets reduce friction drag in water — the same riblet geometry that reduces bacterial adhesion also reduces the force water exerts on a moving shark, linking animal adaptation to forces.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptations that aid survival
curriculum_links.how: The dermal denticles of sharks serve two purposes simultaneously — reducing drag and preventing bacteria from anchoring — illustrating how a single evolved structure can confer multiple survival advantages.

image_idea: A highly magnified view of shark skin showing the tiny ridged tooth-like scales, placed beside a close-up of the Sharklet pattern — the diamond-shaped ridges that copy those scales.

title: The beetle that drinks the fog
creature: Namib desert beetle (Stenocara gracilipes) and several desert plants
where_you_might_see_it: The Namib is one of the world's oldest and driest deserts, running along the Atlantic coast of southern Africa. Almost no rain falls there — yet every morning, a cold sea fog rolls in from the ocean. The beetle that lives there has found a way to drink that fog. In Britain, you might notice something similar on a cold morning: tiny water droplets forming on a spider's web or on a car windscreen. That's the same process — water from the air condensing onto a cold surface.
natures_problem: There is almost no rain in the Namib Desert. But there is fog — a thin, misty cloud that drifts in from the cold Atlantic Ocean most mornings. How can a beetle drink something as wispy as fog?
natures_solution: The beetle stands on top of a sand dune with its back tilted into the wind. Its back is covered in a pattern of tiny bumps and smooth channels. The bumps attract water — fog droplets land on them and stick. The channels are waxy and water-repelling, so once a droplet grows big enough, it rolls quickly along the channel all the way down to the beetle's mouth. It's like the beetle has its own tiny water-collecting machine built into its skin.
what_people_made: Engineers inspired by the beetle — and by desert plants like cactus spines and mosses that use similar tricks — have built large mesh nets that collect fog in the same way. In Morocco, a system of 31 nets the size of tennis courts collects around 37,000 litres of clean drinking water on foggy days. This water is piped to 1,300 people in 16 remote Berber villages in the mountains, where there is no other reliable water source. Similar nets have been installed in Chile and other dry coastal countries. The nano-scale patterns from the beetle are still being refined — future nets may collect even more water by copying the beetle's surface more precisely.
try_this: On a cold morning, look at a spider's web outside. Where do the droplets form — on every thread, or on particular parts of the web? Why do you think some parts collect more water than others?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: States of matter — condensation and the water cycle
curriculum_links.how: The Namib beetle collects water by condensing fog droplets on its back — a vivid, organism-scale demonstration of condensation that makes the abstract concept concrete for Year 4 pupils.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Locational knowledge and human and physical geography — desert climate zones, water scarcity, and the water cycle
curriculum_links.how: The beetle lives in the Namib desert, one of the world's driest places, yet harvests water from coastal fog — a powerful geographical story linking desert climate zones, water scarcity, and the physical processes of the water cycle.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — how surface properties can be used to collect water
curriculum_links.how: The beetle's alternating water-attracting and water-repelling surfaces work together to collect and channel water — showing pupils that surface properties at a tiny scale can solve a large practical problem.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Human geography — water supply, sustainable development, and global challenges
curriculum_links.how: Beetle-inspired fog-harvesting nets are being used to provide clean water in arid regions of Africa and South America without any power source, connecting geographical knowledge of water scarcity to real humanitarian innovation.

image_idea: The Namib beetle on a sand dune, back tilted into the fog, with a close-up inset showing water droplets forming on the tiny bumps of its back and running down channels — beside a photograph of a large fog-collecting net strung between poles in a misty mountain landscape.

title: The mussel's miracle glue
creature: Common mussel (Mytilus edulis) and related species
where_you_might_see_it: Common mussels are found all around the British coastline — clustered on rocks, harbour walls, and piers wherever the tide comes and goes. Next time you're at the seaside, look for dark blue-black shells in bunches on exposed rocks. Tug gently at one: you'll feel the tough, hair-like threads anchoring it firmly to the rock, even as waves crash over it. Those threads are one of the strongest natural glues in the world — and they work underwater.
natures_problem: A mussel lives in one of the toughest places imaginable: on a rock being battered by powerful waves, all day and all night, in cold salty seawater. If it lets go, it will be dashed to pieces. But ordinary glue dissolves in water — it can't do the job.
natures_solution: The mussel makes its own special glue from proteins produced in its foot. It presses its foot against the rock and secretes these proteins, which seep into the tiniest gaps in the rock surface and grip tight. The special ingredient in the proteins first clears away the thin film of water on the rock — creating a brief dry patch — and then bonds powerfully to the rock itself. No manufactured glue has managed to do this as well as a mussel.
what_people_made: Scientists have studied these mussel proteins carefully and started making versions of them in the laboratory. One mussel-inspired surgical glue can seal a bleeding wound in under a minute — in wet, bloody tissue where ordinary stitches and staples can be difficult to use. Because it's made from proteins, the body can safely break it down once the wound has healed. Research is still ongoing, but mussel-inspired materials could one day make surgery safer, quicker, and gentler.
try_this: Try to get two smooth tiles or pieces of plastic to stick together using ordinary PVA glue — once dry, does it hold? Now get them wet and try again. What happens? Now you understand exactly why the mussel's wet-grip glue is so extraordinary.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — comparing how materials behave under different conditions
curriculum_links.how: Mussels glue themselves to wet rocks where synthetic adhesives fail — a clear, testable comparison that introduces the idea that some natural materials have properties our manufactured equivalents have not yet matched.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptation to challenging habitats
curriculum_links.how: The mussel's byssus threads and wet adhesive are evolutionary adaptations to life in the wave-battered intertidal zone — an excellent example of a tough environment driving an extraordinary biological solution.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Living things and their habitats — how animals are suited to their habitat
curriculum_links.how: Common mussels live in one of the most physically demanding UK habitats — pounded by waves on rocky shores — and their attachment mechanism explains how they survive where most animals could not.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Technical knowledge — understanding how new materials inspired by nature solve design problems
curriculum_links.how: Mussel-inspired surgical glues that seal wounds in saltwater conditions show pupils a direct line from observing how a common UK shore animal clings to rock, to a medical invention that saves lives.

image_idea: A cluster of mussels on a wave-splashed rock, with a close-up of the tough, golden-brown threads anchoring one shell to the stone — beside a diagram showing how the threads grip at the molecular scale.

title: The shrimp with the world's most powerful punch
where_you_might_see_it: Mantis shrimps live in warm tropical oceans — they're not found in UK waters. But they are some of the most extraordinary-looking animals on Earth: their bodies are covered in vivid blues, greens, and oranges, a bit like a living jewel. If you ever visit an aquarium you might see one — look out for tanks with special thick glass, because a mantis shrimp can smash a normal aquarium pane with a single strike.
natures_problem: The peacock mantis shrimp hunts crabs and snails by smashing their shells open. To do that it needs to deliver an incredibly powerful punch — far faster and harder than anything a creature its size should be able to manage. But if it punched that hard with an ordinary limb, it would shatter its own club in the process.
natures_solution: The mantis shrimp's clubbing limb is built like a carefully engineered shield. Inside, it has layers of mineralised fibres arranged in a spiral — like a very tightly wound spring or the layers in a croissant, but twisted round and round. When a crack tries to form from an impact, it has to follow the spiral, twisting and turning instead of going straight through. By the time it's finished twisting, the energy of the impact has been used up. The club can strike thousands of times and never crack.
what_people_made: Materials scientists at a university in California studied this spiral-layered structure very carefully. They then made carbon fibre panels — the material used in racing cars, aircraft, and cycle helmets — with layers arranged in the same spiral pattern instead of the usual criss-cross. The spiral-layered panels were about 20% tougher than normal panels using exactly the same materials. The same amount of carbon fibre, arranged differently, becomes harder to smash. That could mean lighter, safer helmets and aircraft panels.
try_this: Take a sheet of paper and try to tear it in a straight line. Now fold a piece of paper into many diagonal layers and try to tear through all of them at once. Which is harder? The mantis shrimp's spiral layers work on the same principle — every layer the crack meets is at a different angle, and that makes it very hard for the crack to keep going.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Forces — impact forces and how materials absorb them
curriculum_links.how: The mantis shrimp delivers a punch faster than a bullet yet its club never cracks — pupils can explore how the spiral internal structure of the club distributes and absorbs impact forces, connecting directly to forces topics.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — how the structure of a material affects its strength and toughness
curriculum_links.how: The mantis shrimp's club is made of the same materials as other animals' shells yet is far tougher, because its layers are arranged in a spiral — showing that the same substance, arranged differently, can behave in a completely different way.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Animals including humans — animal feeding and predator adaptations
curriculum_links.how: The peacock mantis shrimp smashes crab shells with its club to access food — an extraordinary predator adaptation that brings animal feeding strategies vividly to life and prompts questions about why no other animal has evolved a similar weapon.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Technical knowledge — selecting and evaluating materials based on their properties
curriculum_links.how: Aerospace engineers have copied the mantis shrimp's layered structure to make lighter, tougher helmets and aircraft panels, showing pupils how a deep understanding of a material's internal arrangement leads to better-designed products.

image_idea: A vivid close-up of a peacock mantis shrimp mid-strike, beside a cross-section diagram of its club showing the spiral layers — and next to that, a cross-section of a carbon fibre panel built with the same spiral arrangement.

title: The owl that flies in silence
creature: Barn owl (Tyto alba) and related species
where_you_might_see_it: Barn owls live all across Britain and can be seen quartering over fields and meadows at dusk, their white heart-shaped faces ghostly in the fading light. Unlike most birds, a flying barn owl makes almost no sound at all — you can sometimes watch one pass just a few metres away without hearing a single wingbeat. That silence is not an accident.
natures_problem: Owls hunt small mammals — mice and voles — by sound. They can hear a mouse rustling in the grass from thirty metres away. But if the owl's wings made a whooshing noise when it flew, the sound of its own flight would drown out the tiny sounds of its prey below. The owl needs to fly in complete silence.
natures_solution: Barn owl feathers have three clever features working together. The leading edge of each large feather is fringed with tiny comb-like serrations, like the teeth of a very fine comb. These break up the rush of air into smaller, quieter swirls. The upper surface of the feathers is covered in soft, velvety hairs that muffle any remaining sound. And the trailing edge of each feather is ragged and wispy, smoothing the turbulent wake behind the wing. Together, these three things cut the sound of flight to almost nothing.
what_people_made: Engineers at Cambridge University studied barn owl feathers and showed that the comb-like serrations alone could reduce the noise of a blade moving through the air by up to 10 decibels — that's about the same difference as a quiet conversation compared to a normal one. Wind turbine companies have started fitting serrated, comb-like edges to their turbine blades, cutting the noise they make by up to half. This matters because noise is one of the main reasons people object to wind farms being built near their homes — quieter turbines can be built in more places, generating more clean electricity.
try_this: Listen very carefully the next time a bird flies past you quickly. Can you hear the wings? Now think: if you were hunting by listening for tiny sounds, what would happen to your hearing if your own wings were noisy? How would you need to evolve?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Sound — how sound travels and what affects its loudness
curriculum_links.how: Barn owl feathers suppress flight noise through their physical structure — a remarkable real-world demonstration that sound can be reduced by changing a surface's texture, directly linking to Year 4 study of sound and vibration.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptation and predator-prey relationships
curriculum_links.how: Silent flight is a hunting adaptation — owls that make less noise catch more prey — making this a clear example of how natural selection drives extraordinary specialisation in an animal pupils are likely to have heard or seen locally.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — evaluate and improve a product by studying its natural equivalent
curriculum_links.how: Serrated turbine-blade edges copied from owl feathers halve the noise of wind farms, giving pupils a concrete case of a real-world DT problem — public opposition to noisy turbines — solved by observing a British bird.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Human and physical geography — renewable energy and land use
curriculum_links.how: Quieter turbine blades made possible by copying the barn owl can be sited closer to villages, directly connecting pupils' geographical understanding of energy supply and land use decisions to a nature-inspired design solution.

image_idea: A barn owl in low flight over a field, wings fully spread, with a close-up inset of the comb-like serrations on the leading edge of a feather — beside a wind turbine blade showing the same serrated profile along its edge.

title: The burr that invented Velcro
creature: Greater burdock / lesser burdock (Arctium lappa / Arctium minus)
where_you_might_see_it: Burdock is a common British plant found along footpaths, hedgerows, and the edges of woods — especially on disturbed ground. In late summer and autumn, its round, spiky seed heads ripen into burrs that catch on clothing and animal fur. If you've ever come home from a walk with a dog covered in prickly brown balls, you've already met burdock. The burrs are a nuisance — but they're also one of the most important ideas in the history of invention.
natures_problem: Burdock is a plant, and plants can't walk. So how does burdock spread its seeds away from the parent plant to find new places to grow?
natures_solution: Each burdock burr is covered in hundreds of tiny hooks, each one curving over at the tip like a very small shepherd's crook. When an animal brushes past, these hooks catch on loops of fur or fabric and the burr hitches a ride — sometimes for miles — before eventually falling off. The plant uses passing animals as its transport system, and the hooks are its ticket.
what_people_made: In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral came home from a walk in the mountains to find his dog covered in burdock burrs. Instead of just pulling them off and grumbling, he looked at one under a microscope. He saw the tiny hooks very clearly, and he wondered: could you make a fastener that worked the same way? It took him ten years, but in the early 1950s he created what we now call Velcro — one side covered in tiny hooks, the other in tiny loops. Press them together and they grip; pull them apart and they release cleanly. Today Velcro is used on shoes, bags, spacecraft, and surgical equipment all over the world.
try_this: Find a burdock plant on an autumn walk and collect a few burrs (with gloves if you like!). Under a magnifying glass, look closely at the hook tips. Can you see how they curve over? Now press one onto a woolly jumper and pull it off gently. You've just re-enacted the moment that gave George de Mestral his idea.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Plants — seed dispersal and plant structures
curriculum_links.how: Burdock burrs attach to animal fur to hitch a ride and disperse seeds away from the parent plant — the hook structure that inspired Velcro is, first and foremost, a seed-dispersal mechanism, making this the most accessible entry point for KS2 plant biology.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — how natural selection shapes plant structures
curriculum_links.how: The burdock burr's hooked structure was not designed to inspire fasteners — it evolved to grip fur as a seed-dispersal strategy — a vivid illustration of how natural selection produces structure and function that humans later recognise as useful.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — understanding how products are invented and improved
curriculum_links.how: Velcro is the canonical biomimicry story: George de Mestral noticed burrs on his dog's fur, looked closely, and invented one of the world's most widely used fasteners — a story all primary pupils can follow and that shows design as an act of careful observation.

curriculum_links.subject: English
curriculum_links.topic: Writing — narrative and biographical writing, stories of invention
curriculum_links.how: The Velcro origin story is an ideal subject for biographical or narrative writing — a short walk in the Alps, a curious observation, ten years of work — giving younger KS2 pupils a real, true story of invention to retell or dramatise.

image_idea: A close-up of a burdock burr caught on a woollen jumper, beside a hugely magnified image of a single hook from the burr, beside the surface of Velcro showing the matching hook-and-loop structure — three images, one idea.

title: The boxy fish and the low-drag car
where_you_might_see_it: Yellow boxfish live in tropical coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific — the warm, shallow oceans around the Philippines, Indonesia, and Australia. They're not UK animals, but you might see one in a public aquarium. Young ones are bright yellow with black spots and almost perfectly cube-shaped — it looks as though nature made a mistake and forgot to give this fish a streamlined body. But watch it move through the water and you'll see it's surprisingly nimble.
natures_problem: The boxfish lives in a coral reef, where it needs to twist and turn through tight gaps without bumping into things. Its bony box-shaped shell protects it from predators, but that same shape seems like it should make swimming very difficult.
natures_solution: The boxfish moves remarkably well despite its shape. Engineers at Mercedes-Benz measured how much resistance the boxfish body created in a wind tunnel and found the number was very low for a shape that boxy. The rounded curves of its carapace — its bony outer shell — seem to guide the water around it smoothly. Scientists are still debating exactly why it works so well: it turns out that rather than being naturally stable like a boat, the boxfish is actually quite wobbly, and uses its fins constantly to keep course. It may be that the real secret is the fins, not the shell — and the full story isn't settled yet. Science often works this way: a first idea turns out to be more complicated than it seemed.
what_people_made: In 2005, Mercedes-Benz engineers used the outer shape of the boxfish as the starting point for a concept car called the Bionic. Working from the fish's proportions, they designed a car body with a drag coefficient of 0.19 — exceptionally slippery for a full-sized family car at the time. They also used a method inspired by how bones grow to make the car's internal structure lighter and stronger. Some of the ideas from that project were later used in real production cars. The boxfish story also teaches us something important about science: even when a first idea turns out to be incomplete, it can still lead to genuinely useful discoveries.
try_this: Find a small cardboard box and a rounded pebble of about the same size. Hold each one in front of a fan or out of a moving car window (carefully, with an adult!). Which shape creates more resistance? Can you feel a difference? Now think: could a rounded box be more slippery than it looks?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Forces — drag, streamlining, and resistance
curriculum_links.how: The yellow boxfish looks box-shaped yet moves efficiently through water — a counter-intuitive hook for exploring how the relationship between shape and drag is more complex than it first appears, enriching Year 5 forces work.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Animals including humans — animal movement and body structures in aquatic habitats
curriculum_links.how: The boxfish navigates coral reefs with precise, agile movements despite its rigid bony shell — a striking example of how an animal's body structure relates to its habitat and movement, and how stability can be achieved in unexpected ways.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Design — evaluating designs using evidence and testing
curriculum_links.how: The Mercedes Bionic story also illustrates that biomimicry must be grounded in accurate science — later research showed the boxfish story was more complicated than first thought — modelling for pupils the importance of testing and questioning design claims.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Human and physical geography — transport, fuel efficiency, and sustainability
curriculum_links.how: A car designed around a fish shape that uses significantly less fuel than conventional designs connects DT thinking to geographical concepts of resource use, transport, and the environmental impact of how things are made.

image_idea: A bright yellow boxfish in a coral reef beside the sleek, rounded profile of the Mercedes Bionic concept car — two shapes that look very different yet share the same underlying curves.

title: The spider's thread stronger than steel
creature: Orb-weaver spiders, principally golden silk orb-weaver (Nephila spp.) and garden cross spider (Araneus diadematus)
where_you_might_see_it: The garden cross spider is one of Britain's most familiar spiders — large, with a distinctive white cross on its abdomen, spinning beautiful orb webs in hedges and garden shrubs every autumn. On a dewy morning, look for the spiral of sticky threads glistening with droplets. The radial threads running out from the centre — the 'spokes' — are made of a different silk: dry, incredibly strong, and not sticky at all. Those threads are some of the toughest natural fibres on Earth.
natures_problem: A spider needs to spin a web that will catch flying insects without breaking. But the web has to be light enough for the spider to carry, flexible enough not to shatter when an insect hits it, and strong enough to hold a struggling creature until the spider can reach it.
natures_solution: The radial threads of an orb web are made of a silk that is stronger than steel wire of the same thickness and can stretch by a third of its length before snapping. That combination — very strong AND very stretchy — is extraordinarily rare in nature or in manufacturing. The spider produces two different silk proteins and spins them together into a single thread inside its body, pulling the thread through a tiny tube that arranges the proteins into a structure that gives both stiffness and springiness at once. No factory has yet managed to copy this spinning process precisely.
what_people_made: Scientists have decoded the recipe for spider silk proteins and can now grow them using bacteria and yeast in fermentation tanks — a bit like brewing beer, but making silk instead of alcohol. Companies in Germany, Japan, and the United States are turning this laboratory silk into real fibres used in biodegradable trainers, luxury watch straps, car interiors, and experimental medical sutures that dissolve safely inside the body once a wound has healed. Because the silk breaks down naturally, products made from it can be composted rather than adding to landfill. Spider silk is still expensive to make at scale, but scientists are getting closer to matching what the spider does every day for free.
try_this: Find a garden cross spider's web on a dewy autumn morning. Touch the radial 'spoke' threads with a twig — notice they are dry and very springy, not sticky. Now touch the spiral threads gently — they are sticky and stretch much more. The spider uses different silks for different jobs. Can you work out which threads are the load-bearing ones and which ones catch the prey?

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Properties and changes of materials — comparing the properties of natural and synthetic materials
curriculum_links.how: Spider silk is stronger than steel yet lighter than nylon, and biodegrades safely — a powerful example for comparing properties of natural and manufactured materials and exploring what makes a material suitable for a given purpose.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Animals including humans — how animals produce useful structures for survival
curriculum_links.how: The orb-weaver spider spins a web with radial load-bearing threads and spiral sticky threads, each made of different silk with different properties — an accessible, garden-familiar example of an animal producing specialised materials to survive and catch food.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptations and the diversity of life
curriculum_links.how: Different spider species have evolved different silk types for different purposes — dragline, sticky, egg-sac, swathing — illustrating how natural selection drives material specialisation and how diversity within one group of organisms can be enormously rich.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Technical knowledge — selecting materials for performance, sustainability, and function
curriculum_links.how: Synthetic spider-silk fibres are being used in biodegradable trainers and medical sutures, showing pupils that copying how nature makes materials — rather than just what they look like — can lead to products that are both high-performing and environmentally responsible.

image_idea: A garden cross spider in the centre of its dewy orb web on an autumn morning, with a close-up inset of the radial silk thread under magnification — beside a spool of manufactured spider-silk fibre from a fermentation laboratory.

title: The bee that pulls pollen with static
where_you_might_see_it: Any sunny British garden in summer. Watch a bee bumble from flower to flower over the lavender, the foxgloves or the bramble blossom, and look at how it lands already dusted with yellow pollen. By the time it flies home, its furry body and the little baskets on its back legs are heavy with it.
natures_problem: A flower's pollen is a fine, light dust. A bee needs to gather as much of it as possible, as fast as possible — but loose dust blows away on the breeze and is hard to collect from a flower you are only just landing on.
natures_solution: As a bee flies, its tiny hairs rub against the air and build up a small positive charge of static electricity — the very same kind you make by rubbing a balloon on a woolly jumper. Flowers, rooted to the damp ground, carry a slightly negative charge. Because opposite charges pull towards each other, the pollen actually leaps up through the air onto the bee before it has even touched the flower, and clings to its hairy body. Cleverer still, a flower's charge changes for a little while after a bee has visited — so the next bee can sense it has just been emptied and not waste time landing.
what_people_made: People use exactly the same trick to paint things — but we worked it out entirely on our own, long before anyone knew bees did it. In an electrostatic sprayer, the paint droplets are given an electric charge and the object being painted is given the opposite charge. The paint is pulled towards the object and even wraps around to the back, with almost none wasted. Factories paint cars and bicycles this way, and farmers use charged sprays so the droplets cling to every side of a leaf. Nobody copied the bee: engineers invented electric spray-painting in the 1940s, and scientists only discovered the bee's static-pollen trick in 2013. The bee simply got there about a hundred million years first.
try_this: Rub a balloon on a woolly jumper for a few seconds, then hold it just above some tiny scraps of torn-up tissue paper or a sprinkle of dried herbs. Watch the little bits jump UP onto the balloon without being touched. That leap is the same invisible pull a bee uses to lift pollen off a flower.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Electricity — static electricity and how charges attract
curriculum_links.how: A living, watchable example of static attraction: the bee builds a charge like a rubbed balloon and the opposite-charged pollen jumps to it, bringing the idea of charges off the page and into the garden.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Plants — the role of flowers in the life cycle, including pollination
curriculum_links.how: Shows pollination from the bee's side: how a bee gathers and carries pollen between flowers, and why flowers and bees fit together so well.

image_idea: A honeybee covered in golden pollen, hovering just above a purple foxglove flower, the fine hairs on its body visible, with a few grains of pollen lifting up from the flower towards it.

title: The body's shortcut that acts before you think
creature: Human (Homo sapiens) — and every animal with a backbone
where_you_might_see_it: In your own body, every day. The hand you snatch back from a hot pan before it even hurts. The blink when something flies towards your eye. The way your leg kicks when a doctor taps just below your kneecap — a kick you cannot stop even if you try.
natures_problem: Some dangers happen far too fast to think about. A message takes time to travel all the way up to the brain, wait for it to decide 'what shall I do?', and travel all the way back. In that time, you could already be burned.
natures_solution: For the most urgent jobs, the body takes a shortcut called a reflex. The 'danger!' signal races only as far as the spinal cord — the thick bundle of nerves running up your back — which fires the order 'pull away!' straight back to the muscle, skipping the brain altogether. It saves a fraction of a second, and that fraction is enough to save you from a burn. You feel the pain a moment later, once the slower message reaches your brain.
what_people_made: Engineers build this very same shortcut into machines — though they worked it out for themselves, not by studying our nerves. A circuit breaker snaps the electricity off the instant too much flows, without waiting for a person to decide. A car's airbag fires by itself in a crash, and many cars can brake on their own if something darts in front. All of them skip the slow 'thinking' part and act at once, exactly as a reflex does. For the fastest, most important jobs, 'act now, think later' is simply the best design — whether you are a body or a machine.
try_this: Ask someone to hold a ruler straight up and let go without warning, while you hold your finger and thumb ready at the bottom. Try to pinch it as it falls. The distance it drops before you catch it is your reaction time — the time a signal needs to go up to your brain and back. A true reflex would be even quicker, because it never bothers the brain at all.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Electricity — the body's electrical signals and automatic switches
curriculum_links.how: Links the idea of electrical signals and switches to the body: a reflex is a tiny circuit that switches on a muscle automatically, just like a switch closing in a circuit.

curriculum_links.subject: Design & Technology
curriculum_links.topic: Electrical systems and control — automatic responses
curriculum_links.how: A real-world way in to control and sensing: machines, like bodies, can be built to respond to danger automatically without a person deciding each time.

image_idea: A child's hand pulling quickly back from the orange flame of a candle, with a few small curved motion lines showing the fast movement. Friendly, simple, not frightening.

title: The beetle that makes light without heat
creature: Glow-worm (Lampyris noctiluca) — which is really a beetle, not a worm
where_you_might_see_it: On warm, still nights in June and July, on grassy banks and hedge bottoms in southern England. Low to the ground, a female glow-worm shines a steady greenish light from the tip of her tail to call a flying male down to her. You need a really dark spot and a few minutes for your eyes to adjust — no torch.
natures_problem: An ordinary light, like an old-fashioned bulb, throws away most of its energy as heat — touch one and it is hot. A tiny beetle could never make light that way: the heat would harm her, and she has nowhere near enough energy to spare.
natures_solution: The glow-worm makes 'cold light'. Inside the tip of her body, a chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen and gives off light with almost no heat at all — nearly every scrap of energy becomes light instead of warmth. It is one of the most efficient lights anywhere in nature.
what_people_made: People make cold light too, in the glow sticks you bend and snap at fairs and on bonfire night. Snapping the stick mixes two chemicals that react and shine — no battery, no heat, just like the glow-worm. We did not copy the beetle to invent them; chemists found their own glowing chemicals. But nature had been lighting up summer hedgerows with cold light for millions of years before the very first glow stick was ever cracked.
try_this: On a warm, dark night in July, look along grassy banks and hedge bottoms in the south of England for a tiny green light close to the ground — a female glow-worm. Hold a snapped glow stick beside a warm yellow torch or lamp: feel how the glow stick stays cool while a bulb gets hot. That is the glow-worm's trick.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Light — sources that make their own light
curriculum_links.how: A living light source: the glow-worm makes her own light rather than reflecting it, a vivid example when sorting things that give out light from things that only reflect it.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Living things and their habitats — life cycles and reproduction
curriculum_links.how: The female's glow is a signal to attract a mate, connecting a striking adaptation to how living things find each other and reproduce.

image_idea: A female glow-worm (Lampyris noctiluca), a small soft-brown beetle-like insect, on a green grass stem, the tip of her tail glowing with a soft green light.

title: The fish that powered the very first battery
where_you_might_see_it: Not in Britain — the electric eel lives in the slow, muddy rivers and swamps of South America, where the water is too murky to see far. You can meet one, though, in the tanks of many large aquariums.
natures_problem: In dark, muddy water you cannot rely on your eyes to find a meal or fight off an attacker. The electric eel needed another way to reach out and touch the world around it.
natures_solution: Most of the eel's long body is packed with special cells stacked in their thousands, one on top of another, like a tall pile of tiny flat batteries. Each cell makes only a feeble amount of electricity, but stacked together and fired at once they add up to a powerful shock — enough to stun a fish or warn off a much bigger animal.
what_people_made: This one really was copied from nature, on purpose. Around the year 1800, the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta was puzzling over how electric fish made their shock. He built a tall stack of metal discs separated by damp cardboard — deliberately copying the stacked layers inside the fish — and it gave out a steady flow of electricity. It was the world's first battery, and he even called it an 'artificial electric organ'. Every battery since, in your torch, your toys and your phone, is a grandchild of that fishy idea.
try_this: Make a battery from a lemon. Push a copper coin into one side and a galvanised (zinc-coated) nail into the other, then touch both to a small bulb or a tongue-tingle. Now join two or three lemons in a row — more 'cells' stacked together make more power, exactly the way the eel stacks its cells.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Electricity — cells, batteries and simple circuits
curriculum_links.how: Brings the cell or battery in a circuit to life: the eel is a living stack of cells, a memorable way in to where the electricity in a circuit comes from.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Electricity — voltage and the number of cells
curriculum_links.how: The eel adds many small cells together to make a bigger shock — exactly the Year 6 idea that more cells, or higher voltage, give a stronger effect such as a brighter lamp.

image_idea: An electric eel (Electrophorus electricus), a long, dark olive-green eel-shaped fish with a rounded head, swimming gently, with a faint soft glow around its body to suggest electricity.

title: The butterfly with invisible wings
where_you_might_see_it: Not in Britain — the glasswing lives in the rainforests of Central and South America. You can sometimes spot one in a tropical butterfly house at a zoo or garden. Its wings are see-through, like tiny panes of glass with a dark frame.
natures_problem: See-through wings should be the perfect way to hide. But ordinary clear surfaces, like glass or water, catch the light and flash with bright reflections — and a flash of glare would give the butterfly away to a hungry bird in an instant.
natures_solution: Looked at under a microscope, the clear part of the wing is covered in millions of tiny bumps, far too small to see, all spaced very evenly. These bumps let the light pass straight through instead of bouncing back, so the wing hardly reflects at all. With no tell-tale glare, the butterfly stays truly hard to see.
what_people_made: Scientists studied those tiny bumps and copied them on purpose to make 'anti-reflective' surfaces — glass and screens that do not bounce light back at you. The same idea helps phone and tablet screens you can still read in bright sunshine, camera lenses that flare less, and solar panels that soak up more light instead of wasting it as glare. This one was deliberately copied from the butterfly's wing.
try_this: Tilt a phone or tablet screen under a bright light or near a window and watch it flash with reflections. That glare is exactly what the glasswing's wing avoids — and it is why a shiny screen is so hard to read in sunshine. Look for screens or glasses that are described as 'anti-glare' and see how much less they shine back.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Light — how light reflects off surfaces
curriculum_links.how: A surprising twist on reflection: most surfaces bounce light back, but the glasswing's wing is built to stop reflections, sharpening pupils' idea of what reflected light is.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptation and camouflage
curriculum_links.how: Transparency as camouflage: see-through wings are an adaptation that helps the butterfly avoid being seen, a vivid example of a body suited to its surroundings.

image_idea: A glasswing butterfly (Greta oto) resting on a green leaf, its wings clear and see-through like glass, edged with a dark brown border tinged with orange-red.

title: The beetle with a built-in spray gun
where_you_might_see_it: A small ground beetle found on chalky grassland in southern England, often hiding under stones by day. You are unlikely to catch it in the act, but when something threatens it, it fires a hot, stinging spray from its tail end with a sharp popping sound.
natures_problem: A small beetle is an easy meal for frogs, birds and spiders, and it cannot outrun most of them. It needs a way to startle and sting an attacker far bigger than itself, and buy enough time to escape.
natures_solution: The beetle keeps two harmless liquids in separate stores inside its body. When it is attacked, it squirts them together into a tiny chamber where they react, heat up to almost boiling, and burst out as a fast spray — fired in rapid pulses, like a string of tiny pops, and aimed with surprising accuracy at whatever is bothering it.
what_people_made: Engineers studied how the beetle fires its spray in quick pulses and copied the idea to design better sprays and engines. Copying the beetle's pulsing chamber helped make finer mist from medicine inhalers and fire extinguishers, and cleaner bursts of fuel inside car engines — sprays that travel further and waste less. This one was studied and copied on purpose, the beetle showing the way.
try_this: Hold your thumb half over the end of a squeezy water bottle and squeeze in short, sharp bursts instead of one long squirt. Notice how the pulsing spray throws the water further and finer. That pulsing is the beetle's trick — lots of small bursts beat one weak dribble.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: States of matter — mixing liquids, heating and gases
curriculum_links.how: Two liquids mix, react and heat up to make a hot gassy spray — a dramatic example of materials changing when they are mixed and heated.

curriculum_links.subject: Science
curriculum_links.topic: Evolution and inheritance — adaptation for defence
curriculum_links.how: An extraordinary defence adaptation: the beetle's chemical spray is a body feature shaped to help it survive, fitting the Year 6 idea of adaptation to an environment and its dangers.

image_idea: A bombardier beetle (Brachinus crepitans) standing on a small grey stone, with glossy blue-black wing cases and an orange-red head and legs, a tiny puff of vapour shown coming from its tail end.
